1 Outline

Scales

7-point Likert Scale. 8 = Not Applicable.

  1. Check distributions of scores for each item(including 8 and missing).
  2. Check missing values (percentage missing in each survey item, and missing patterns across all items and all scales). 2.1 Explore demographic differences between the missing vs. non-missing groups. 2.2 Explore demographic difference between the “actual missing (NA)” group vs. people who chose 8.
  3. Compute mean scores and standard deviations for each item after removing NAs and 8.

Demographics

  1. Attach labels to the demographic (checkbox) dummy variables (i.e. “collapsing” multiple dummies into a categorical variable)
  2. Check distributions
  3. Check missing values and missing patterns
  4. Compute summary statistics

3 Demographics

3.1 Site and Role

  • Primary site site_oath_v2: categorical (factor)

  • Role role_oath_v2: categorical (factor)

    • role_oath_spec if role_oath_v2 = 7: text

  • Number of years in current role years_role_oath_v2: categorical (factor)

  • Number of years at THP years_employed_thp_v2: categorical (factor)

  • Have academic appoint academic_appt: binary

demog_role <- raw.data %>% 
  select(record_id, site_oath_v2, role_oath_v2, years_role_oath_v2, 
         years_employed_thp_v2, academic_appt) %>% 
  # convert to factor and attach text labels for summary
  mutate(
    site_oath_v2 = factor(site_oath_v2,
                          levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
                          labels = c("Credit Valley Hospital", 
                                     "Missisauga Hospital", 
                                     "Queensway Health Centre", 
                                     "Other")
                          ),
    role_oath_v2 = factor(role_oath_v2,
                          levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7),
                          labels = c("Administrative/Consultant",
                                     "Director",
                                     "Manager",
                                     "Professional Staff",
                                     "Senior Leadership",
                                     "Supervisor/Team Leader",
                                     "Other")
                          ),
    years_role_oath_v2 = factor(years_role_oath_v2,
                                levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                                labels = c("< 1 year",
                                           "1-3 years",
                                           "3-6 years",
                                           "6-9 years",
                                           "10+ years")
                                ),
    years_employed_thp_v2 = factor(years_employed_thp_v2,
                                   levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                                   labels = c("< 1 year",
                                              "1-3 years",
                                              "3-6 years",
                                              "6-9 years",
                                              "10+ years")
                                   ),
    academic_appt = factor(academic_appt,
                           levels = c(1, 0),
                           labels = c("Yes", "No"))
  )

4 Missing Values

4.1 Missingness Pattern across Exploration, Exploitation and De-Implementation Surveys

learning.scales <- raw.data %>% 
  select(starts_with(c("explore", "exploit", "deimplement")))

gg_miss_upset(learning.scales, nsets = ncol(learning.scales))

The Learning Ambidexterity scales and De-implementation scale appear to show highly systematic patterns of missingness. The most common pattern is skipping (missing) all questions in all three scales, followed by those who filled out only the exploration survey but missed the exploitation and de-implementation surveys entirely, and finally those who filled out the exploration and exploitation surveys, but not the de-implementation survey.

This suggests missingness is likely driven by an external factor (ex. specific groups of non-respondents, lost interest, or a specific survey is less relevant), rather than missing at random.

gg_miss_upset(demog_role %>% select(-record_id), nsets = ncol(learning.scales))
